question: to the Commission Katri Kulmuni (Renew) Subject:

Regulation (EU) 2024/900 of the European Parliament and of the Council on the transparency and targeting of political advertising entered into force last autumn. As a result, small local branches of political parties, for example, are required to find space on their meeting notices for large QR codes costing EUR 100. They are also required to produce detailed reports. According to the feedback I have received, these rules are widely perceived as being annoying and pointless. Although the regulation does not ban political advertising, Facebook, for example, has already banned paid political advertising altogether, at least in part as a result of the regulation. Political parties are the bedrock of democracy, also in Europe. Many national parties are made up of small local branches whose activities are based on people carrying out voluntary work. They should not have to bear the burden of unnecessary bureaucracy. In general, in a democracy, party activities should not be seen as inherently suspicious, but rather as something worthy of support. In its reply of 29 January 2026 to Merja Kyllönen’s written question (E-004384/2025)1, the Commission stated that it was in contact with stakeholders as it monitors the application of the regulation. The Commission is also planning to revise the EU public procurement directives in the second quarter of 2026. With the above in mind: How does the Commission intend to assess the actual impact that the regulation will have on civil society and establish the extent to which the new rules can effectively prevent electoral interference from outside the EU?
https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-10-2025-004384_EN.html.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.6.2026) Regulation (EU) 2024/900 on the transparency and targeting of political advertising1 establishes common transparency and accountability standards of political advertising services. The guidelines2 adopted by the Commission in October 2025 to support the effective implementation of the Regulation clarify the obligations for sponsors, including political actors, as well as other entities engaging in political advertising activities. Such obligations, primarily relate to declaring political advertising and providing the information necessary for providers of political advertising services to ensure compliance with their transparency or due diligence obligations. In this regard, the guidelines clarify that reporting, labelling and record keeping obligations are only applicable to service providers, not to the political actors or entities requesting such services. The Regulation also contributes to the prevention of electoral interference from outside the EU, by introducing an obligation for third-country service providers to designate a legal representative in one of the Member States where they offer their services, and by prohibiting political advertising service providers from engaging with sponsors from third countries during the three months leading up to any election or referendum in a Member State. Under Article 27 of Regulation (EU) 2024/900, the Commission will submit a report on the evaluation and review of the Regulation to the European Parliament and to the Council within two years after the next elections to the European Parliament. The Commission will also organise, in 2026, an implementation dialogue to draw insights from the application of the rules.
